objective: By the end of this lesson you can decide, to commercial standards, whether you, the airplane, and the flight environment are ready for a flight that may carry paying passengers: assess yourself, prove the airplane is airworthy and equipped for hire, inspect it with the checklist, and keep reassessing the environment and outside pressures.
why: Paying passengers trust you to make the go or no-go call for them. About 85 percent of aviation accidents have been blamed on "failure of the pilot to..." [[24:49|AFH 2-12]], and the preflight assessment is where you catch problems while everyone is still safe on the ground.

prereading.what: Airworthiness records, documents, the visual preflight inspection, fuel and oil, and ramp safety.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 2, 2-1 to 2-14

prereading.label: PHAK 9-7 to 9-12

prereading.label: PHAK 7-27 to 7-29

warmup: Your first paid sightseeing tour leaves in 40 minutes and ends after dark. The landing light is burned out and the passengers are already in the lobby. A private pilot flying friends could defer that light. Can you? What else changes when someone is paying?

key_terms.def: The aircraft conforms to its type design and is in condition for safe operation (14 CFR 3.5(a), as quoted in the AFH).
FAA Form 8100-2. Stays in effect as long as maintenance is done under Parts 21, 43 and 91 and the aircraft stays U.S. registered. Must be displayed where passengers or crew can read it.

Required within the preceding 100 hours of time in service when carrying any person (other than a crewmember) for hire, or giving flight instruction for hire in an airplane you provide. An annual may take its place.
A special airworthiness certificate that lets an aircraft not meeting airworthiness rules, but safe for a specific flight, fly to a place where it can be fixed or inspected.
Aeromedical self-check: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion.
Four hazard buckets: Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures.
Flight Risk Assessment Tool: a form for recording hazards. A numerical FRAT adds points for each hazard into a total score.
The risk level found by crossing likelihood (probable to improbable) with severity (catastrophic to negligible) on a risk matrix.
The fuel-air charge explodes instead of burning smoothly. Using a lower fuel grade than required can cause it; severe detonation can cause engine failure in minutes.
Water that has settled at the bottom of a fuel tank, separated from the fuel above. It can be drained through the sump drains.
Sectional symbol used in crowded areas. Only the highest obstacle in the group is charted.

chunks.title: The preflight assessment, at commercial level

body.p: A preflight assessment looks at five things: the regulations, your readiness to act as PIC, the airplane's condition, the flight environment, and any outside pressures [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. Rushed ground work shrinks your margin of safety [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

"Airworthy" has two parts: the airplane conforms to its type design, and it is in condition for safe operation [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. The owner or operator is primarily responsible for keeping it maintained [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. You, the PIC, decide if it is safe to fly today [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

callout.text: No person may operate a civil aircraft unless it is airworthy. The PIC is responsible for determining whether it is in condition for safe flight, and must discontinue the flight when unairworthy mechanical, electrical, or structural conditions occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]]. The PIC is directly responsible for, and the final authority on, the operation of the aircraft [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]].

body.p: Before every flight you must become familiar with all available information about it. For any flight that includes runway lengths and takeoff and landing distances. For IFR, or a flight not near an airport, it also includes weather, fuel, alternatives, and known ATC delays [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].
What changes when you fly for hire? The rules ask more of you and of the airplane:

head: Item
Private-style flight (not for hire)
Flight carrying a person for hire
rows: At least third class, except under the 61.113(i) conditions [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(a)(3)(i)]]
At least second class to use commercial privileges [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]]
Annual, plus a 100-hour (or annual) within the preceding 100 hours [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]
Not required under Part 91 when not for hire [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]
One electric landing light required [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]]
Over water, beyond power-off gliding distance from shore
Flotation gear for each occupant and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]]
Mitigate risks to medium (green) or lower [[30:39|RMH 5-1]]
Part 121, Part 135 and Part 91 subpart K operations normally preclude serious and high risk operations; hold yourself to that standard [[30:39|RMH 5-1]]

callout.text: The rules don't cover every situation and don't guarantee safety [[30:13|RMH 2-1]]. Professional pilots live by the numbers [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Your passengers can't judge the risk for themselves, so your standards are their protection.

check.q: On a paid tour, who has the final say on whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight: the owner, the mechanic, or you?
check.a: You. The PIC is responsible for determining whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]], and is the final authority on its operation [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]].

chunks.title: Self-assessment: are you fit to fly for hire?

body.p: The RMH splits pilot hazards into two groups: capability and aeromedical [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Capability comes first:

bullets: Qualification: do you hold the certificate, category, class and ratings the flight needs under today's conditions [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]?
Currency: have you logged the takeoffs, landings, approaches and flight review that 14 CFR requires, and is that enough for this flight [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]?

Proficiency: can you really manage the expected conditions? IFR currency earned five months ago may not mean you can fly low ceilings well today. In an unfamiliar airplane, can you run its avionics and systems [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]?

body.p: Then check your body and mind with IMSAFE [[30:23|RMH 3-5]], [[30:24|RMH Figure 3-3]]:

head: IMSAFE
Ask yourself
What the RMH adds
rows: Even mild symptoms can be a hazard [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]
Have I taken prescription or over-the-counter drugs?
Both kinds have side effects that can hurt performance [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]
Pressure from the job, money, health, or family?
Stress affects thinking, behavior, and health [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]
Hangover and dehydration can last longer than 8 hours [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]
Am I tired and not adequately rested?
Sleep fixes only acute fatigue, not chronic fatigue; effects can be subtle [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]

body.p: Some publications use the E for Eating. On a long day of flying, plan your food and water [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

callout.text: No crewmember within 8 hours after any alcoholic beverage, while under the influence, while using a drug that affects your faculties contrary to safety, or with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. You may not act as PIC while you know or have reason to know of a medical condition, or take medication or treatment for one, that would make you unable to meet the medical certificate you need [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]]. For commercial privileges that is at least a second-class medical [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]].

body.p: Legal is not the same as smart or safe [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]. Personal minimums that match your experience lower pilot risk. Raise them in an unfamiliar airplane, and if you doubt the outcome of a flight, consider bringing an instructor or mentor [[30:39|RMH 5-1]].

callout.text: Illness, medication, stress, fatigue, or several weeks without flying? The RMH suggests adding at least 500 feet to your ceiling minimum, as a starting point [[30:17|RMH Figure 2-9]].

check.q: You slept 9 hours last night, but you have been short on sleep all week. Did one good night clear the fatigue hazard?
check.a: Not necessarily. Enough sleep corrects only acute fatigue. Chronic fatigue can have several causes and needs more analysis [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

chunks.title: Is the airplane airworthy? Certificate, records, inspections

body.p: An FAA representative issues the Airworthiness Certificate after the aircraft is inspected, meets Part 21, and is in condition for safe operation [[1:237|PHAK 9-7]]. It must be displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance where passengers or crew can read it [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]].

Look at box 6, Terms and Conditions. The certificate stays in effect as long as maintenance is done under Parts 21, 43 and 91 and the airplane stays registered in the U.S. [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. So the certificate on the wall does not prove the airplane is airworthy today. The records do.
Logbooks are not normally kept in the airplane. Check them, or a summary of airworthy status, before flight [[24:39|AFH 2-2]]. Fix any discrepancy before you go [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

head: Record check
Requirement
Source
rows: If carrying any person (not crew) for hire, or giving flight instruction for hire in an airplane you provide
Tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months
Within 24 calendar months, for IFR in controlled airspace
Inspected within 12 calendar months after the last inspection
Replace or recharge after more than 1 cumulative hour of use, or at 50 percent of useful life
Current status per the Type Certificate Data Sheet

callout.text: ADs are regulatory. Some need repeat action, for example an inspection every 50 hours of time in service. There is no allowance to overfly an AD's hour limit unless the AD itself says so [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

body.p: Documents that must be aboard, attached, or affixed, as appropriate: airworthiness certificate and registration [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)]], operating limitations (AFM/POH, placards, markings) [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]], current weight and balance data, a compass correction card if required, and the data plate. A radio station license is needed only outside the U.S. or over 12,500 pounds [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

callout.text: Twelve calendar months run from any day of a month to the last day of the same month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

check.q: The tour airplane's annual was signed off June 10, 2026. What is the last day it may fly without a new annual?
check.a: June 30, 2027. Twelve calendar months run to the last day of the same month the following year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]], [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].

chunks.title: Flying for hire: what more the airplane needs

body.p: One kind of flight a commercial pilot may fly for an operator is a nonstop sightseeing flight: they begin and end at the same airport and stay within 25 statute miles of it [[60:463|14 CFR 91.147(a)]]. Here is what that kind of flight demands of the airplane.

The 100-hour inspection. Carrying any person other than a crewmember for hire needs an annual or 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours of time in service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. You may go up to 10 hours over, but only while en route to reach a place where the inspection can be done. That extra time counts toward the next 100 hours [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

callout.text: Paying passenger aboard? Check two clocks: the annual date AND the hours left until the next 100-hour [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409]].

head: Flight for hire
Extra equipment required
Rule
rows: Over water and beyond power-off gliding distance from shore
Approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant, and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device

body.p: The RMH notes that a landing light is not required for Part 91 flights not for hire, but a dead landing light still makes night flying more hazardous [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]. For hire at night, it is simply required.

After maintenance. If maintenance may have appreciably changed how the airplane flies, you may not carry anyone but crew until an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private certificate flies it, makes an operational check, and logs the flight. Skip that flight only if ground tests or inspection conclusively show nothing changed [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)-(c)]].

Is it the right airplane? Ask: Is it equipped for this flight? Can it use these runways with a margin? Can it carry this load and reach the altitudes needed? Does it have enough fuel with reserves? Does the fuel delivered match the fuel ordered [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]], [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]? Watch for performance hazards too: range, takeoff and landing distance, altitude, payload, and weight and balance [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

callout.text: Except in an emergency, you may not allow a person who appears intoxicated, or shows signs of being under the influence of drugs (except a medical patient under proper care), to be carried in the aircraft [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(b)]].

check.q: Tonight's paid tour returns after dark. The landing light just burned out. Can you go?
check.a: No. A landing light is required for night VFR when the aircraft is operated for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]], so it can't be deferred under 91.213(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

chunks.title: Something is inoperative: cancel, fix, or defer

body.p: When you find inoperative equipment before flight, you have three choices: cancel the flight, get maintenance before flight, or defer the item [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Deferrals are for problems found before flight, not for failures in flight; in flight you use the AFM/POH procedures [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].
A non-turbine small airplane with no MEL may take off with an item inoperative under 91.213(d) only if the item is NOT [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]:

bullets: Part of the VFR-day type certification instruments and equipment.
Shown as required on the aircraft's equipment list or Kinds of Operations Equipment List for this kind of flight.
Required by 91.205 or any other Part 91 rule for the specific kind of flight. For hire at night, that includes the landing light.
Required to be working by an airworthiness directive.

body.p: Then the item is removed (control placarded, maintenance recorded) or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative," and an appropriately rated pilot, or a person rated to maintain the aircraft, decides it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)-(4)]]. Removal always involves maintenance, so a certificated mechanic must do and record it [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]], [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

If the operator has an MEL and Letter of Authorization, using the MEL becomes mandatory, and the MEL, LOA, preamble, and procedures document must be aboard on every flight [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. If an item can't be deferred (the PHAK's examples are a tachometer, flaps, or stall warning device not listed as deferrable) and repair isn't available, a special flight permit from the FSDO can let you fly it to a repair shop [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]], [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]].

callout.text: Deferring maintenance is not to be taken lightly. Think about how the item affects the flight, especially if other items are also inoperative [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

check.q: Under 91.213(d), who may decide that a deactivated, placarded item is not a hazard?
check.a: A pilot certificated and appropriately rated under Part 61, or a person certificated and appropriately rated to maintain the aircraft [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: the checklist walk-around

head: ACS skill
Standard
rows: Inspect the airplane with reference to an appropriate checklist.
Verify the airplane is in condition for safe flight and conforms to its type design.
Continue to assess the environment for safe flight.

body.p: This Task has no numeric tolerances. Use the AFM/POH checklist, or a third-party checklist based on it; each manufacturer sets its own sequence [[24:42|AFH 2-5]]. A typical flow:

bullets: 1. Records first: inspections, ADs, and inoperative items [[24:40|AFH 2-3]], [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].
2. Walk up slowly: gear alignment, distorted wings, fuselage or tail, skin damage, stains, drips or puddles [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].
3. Documents aboard [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].
4. Door and cabin: door fit and latches, carpet, belts and harnesses, seats locked in their rails, windshield clean and free of cracks and crazing [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

5. Flight deck: gear handle DOWN if retractable, switches OFF, control locks REMOVED, fuel selector works in every position including OFF, trim set, breakers IN. Master ON: compare fuel gauges with what you see in the tanks; test lights and annunciators [[24:42|AFH 2-5]].
6. Instruments: airspeed zero; altimeter within 75 feet of field elevation for IFR; wet compass full of fluid with a legible correction card; mechanical VSI zero [[24:42|AFH 2-5]].

7. Glass panel: reference guide aboard, red Xs clear as sensors come alive, low-level alarms tested, cooling fans working. Allow extra time; this checklist can be long [[24:42|AFH 2-5]], [[24:43|AFH 2-6]].
8. Outside, often counterclockwise from the door: structure, fuel and oil, gear, engine and propeller [[24:43|AFH 2-6]].

head: Where
Defect to look for
Why it matters
rows: Hard to close, poor fit, rough latches
Can mean doorpost misalignment from structural damage [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]
Can give near zero visibility at some sun angles [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]
Stiff, no detents, tank position not legible
Cloudy face, bubbles, partly filled case
Stall fences, slots, vortex generators, boots
Know their proper condition to inspect them [[24:44|AFH 2-7]]
Chipped or flaking paint around rivets
May show a lack of security; refer to a mechanic [[24:48|AFH 2-11]]
Shimmy damper leaks, free play in torque links
Nose gear must be secure and serviced [[24:48|AFH 2-11]]
Oil streaking from hub toward the tip
Exhaust leaks at the cylinder head or cracked stacks [[24:49|AFH 2-12]]
An isolated area of darkened, oxidized paint
May mean that area is overheating [[24:49|AFH 2-12]]

callout.text: On a low-wing or wheel-pant airplane, crouch and use a flashlight. It is still your job to inspect the gear properly [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

check.q: Snow fell overnight and some got inside the spinner openings. Why does that matter?
check.a: The engine, propeller and spinner are balanced around the crankshaft. A small amount of ice or snow inside the spinner can produce damaging vibrations, so make sure it is free of ice [[24:49|AFH 2-12]].

body.p: Without the right fuel quantity, grade, and quality, the engine will likely quit [[24:46|AFH 2-9]]. The three conventional AVGAS grades are dyed: 80/87 red, 100LL blue, 100/130 green. Blue 100LL can be hard to see unless you hold the sample against a white background in good light [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].

bullets: Never use a lower grade than required. Detonation will severely damage the engine in a very short time [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].
Engines certificated for 80/87 run on 100LL if it is approved as an alternate. The reverse is not true [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].
Automobile gas is acceptable only if the airplane has a Supplemental Type Certificate for both airframe and engine [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].
Jet fuel smells like kerosene, feels oily, and is clear or straw colored. A piston engine on jet fuel may run long enough to take off, then fail [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].
Jet fuel trucks carry JET-A placards in white on black [[24:45|AFH 2-8]]. AVGAS is labeled in white letters on red [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]].
AVGAS nozzles are straight. Jet fuel nozzles are flared so they won't fit an AVGAS filler [[24:45|AFH 2-8]], [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

body.p: Fuel contamination accidents are often traced to a poor preflight, fuel poorly filtered from drums or small tanks, airplanes stored with partly filled tanks, and poor maintenance [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]]. Water is the principal contaminant [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]].

head: Water
What it is
What to do
rows: Settled at the bottom of the tank, with a clear line between it and the fuel
Drain it through the sumps. If it froze, drains may be useless: warm the airplane in a hangar, then drain every sump [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]]
Tiny droplets suspended in the fuel; can make fuel look cloudy or hazy
Settles out over time; not all of it can be removed in the field [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]]
Water in solution with the fuel
Removed only by dehydration or by cooling it into entrained and then free water [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]]

bullets: Drain enough from the strainer to be sure you are getting fuel from the tank; water may not show until the lines are drained [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]].
Water can remain in the tanks after the strainer sample runs clean. Only the tank sump drains remove it [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]].
Water in the first sample? Keep sampling until none appears. Significant or repeated water or sediment needs maintenance [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].
Small dark specks mean rubber seals or sealant are breaking down [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].
Fill the tanks after the last flight of the day to limit condensation [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].
Avoid refueling from cans and drums. A worn chamois, or a damp one, won't filter water [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]].
Check vents. A rush of air when you crack a cap can mean a vent problem that leads to fuel starvation [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

body.p: Oil: check it every preflight and at every refueling. Piston engines commonly hold 4 to 8 quarts. Oil that darkens quickly after an oil change, or a sudden change in oil use, needs a mechanic's look [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]. During refueling, take passengers out of the airplane and watch the fueling yourself [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

check.q: The strainer sample is clean, but you have not drained the tank sumps yet. Are you done sampling?
check.a: No. Water may remain in the tanks after the strainer stops showing it; that residual water comes out only through the tank sump drains [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]].

body.p: The environment ("V") covers weather, terrain, airports, airspace, time of day, and more. Weather is the most variable of them [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

head: Factor
What to check
rows: Thunderstorms, icing (including frost, ice, or snow on the parked airplane), low ceilings and visibility, turbulence, and crosswind beyond the airplane's demonstrated value or your ability [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]. Weather may differ from the forecast, so have alternatives [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]
Mountains, high density altitude, and night takeoffs over water [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]. Pick safe altitudes from charts and MEFs in advance [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]
Runway size, wet or snowy runways, approach aids and lighting [[30:25|RMH 3-7]], [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. NOTAMs for closed runways and lights out [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]
Prohibited and restricted areas, ATC delays that burn extra fuel, traffic density [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. TFRs along the route [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]
Hazards are harder to see; a forced landing in the dark; an alternator failure may become a total electrical failure [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]
An engine failure makes nearby airports supremely important [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]. Plan to go around, above, or below a hazard, change the departure time, or cancel [[30:40|RMH 5-2]]

body.p: Obstructions. Many structures can affect your flight below 500 feet AGL, and particularly below 200 feet [[34:159|AIM 7-6-4]]. At and below 200 feet AGL, many power lines and towers are not marked, lit, or charted, and new obstructions may not be on current charts [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4]]. Some towers stand over 2,000 feet AGL, and their guy wires reach about 1,500 feet out, so avoid skeletal structures horizontally by at least 2,000 feet [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4]].

Elkins, West Virginia sits in a valley at 1,987 feet, with terrain and obstacles on both sides as high as 3,631 feet [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. On a clear, calm day the risk is low. At night the same terrain makes an accident more likely [[30:27|RMH 3-9]].

bullets: Obstacles: blue number = top of the obstacle in feet MSL; the number in parentheses below it = height AGL [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]].
UC = the obstacle is under construction or reported but not yet verified [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]].
Group obstacle symbol = only the highest obstacle in a crowded area is shown [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]].
MEF over natural terrain = highest point + 100 feet possible error + 200 feet for uncharted obstacles, rounded up to the next 100 [[2:13|Chart Users' Guide p.13]].

Airport data line: elevation, lighting (*L means lighting limitations exist, such as part-time or pilot-controlled lighting; check the Chart Supplement), longest runway in hundreds of feet, then a frequency; a circled C after it marks the CTAF [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p.15]].

callout.text: Keep assessing. Weather can change drastically over time and distance [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]]. Situational awareness lasts until the airplane is tied down or hangared [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

check.q: You plan to follow a river at low altitude. Why can't you count on the sectional to show every wire?
check.a: Many wires and towers at or below 200 feet AGL are not marked, lit, or charted, and new obstructions may not be on current charts yet [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4]]. Wires often span natural flyways like rivers [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4]].

chunks.title: Risk: PAVE, the FRAT, and the risk matrix

body.p: PAVE sorts hazards into four buckets. Using all four before a flight catches most hazards you will meet [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Find them by looking, by preflight planning, with on-board equipment, by radio, and by postflight inspections [[30:22|RMH 3-4]].

A Flight Risk Assessment Tool (FRAT) records hazards during planning. In a numerical FRAT you pick the hazards that apply and add their points. The total falls into low, caution, or danger ranges [[30:28|RMH 3-10]].

Risk = likelihood x severity. Likelihood: probable, occasional, remote, improbable. Severity: catastrophic, critical, marginal, negligible [[30:34|RMH 4-1]]. Cross them on the matrix to find the composite risk [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].

bullets: Medium (green): go, but still mitigate if you can [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].
Serious (yellow) or high (red): no-go, unless you mitigate so that the next assessment shows medium or low [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].
High risks you can't mitigate mean no-go [[30:39|RMH 5-1]].

head: PAVE area
Ways to mitigate
rows: Personal minimums for your experience, raised in an unfamiliar airplane; IMSAFE; bring an instructor or mentor if in doubt [[30:39|RMH 5-1]]
Add margins to performance data; choose redundant systems or automation; fix discrepancies; do thorough preflight and postflight inspections; carry enough fuel, or plan a fuel stop [[30:39|RMH 5-1]]
Mostly avoidance: go around, above, or below the hazard, change the departure time or date, or cancel [[30:40|RMH 5-2]]

callout.text: Matrix traps: if unsure between two levels, use the more conservative one. Don't skew the inputs toward low risk because you want to go. Recheck the assessment if hazards change before departure [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].

check.q: A hazard is rated "occasional" likelihood and "critical" severity. What composite risk is that, and what does it mean for the flight?
check.a: Serious (yellow). That implies no-go unless you can reduce the risk so the next assessment comes out medium or low [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].

body.p: External pressures come from personal and business reasons: an event at the destination, someone waiting, or a passenger you don't want to let down. They can also start in flight, like a sick passenger [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. Business flights add pressure to complete the "mission" no matter the hazards [[30:26|RMH 3-8]].

Pilots under external pressure sometimes fail to consider the other three hazard categories [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. That is why the PHAK calls managing external pressure the single most important key to risk management, and says it figures into a majority of accidents [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

bullets: Tell people waiting that the flight needs flexibility [[30:40|RMH 5-2]].
For business passengers, manage their expectations and plan other ways for them to travel [[30:40|RMH 5-2]].
Build personal SOPs: time for an extra fuel stop, backup airline reservations, or leaving early enough to drive [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].
Write your personal minimums down. A written set makes it easier to explain tough decisions to passengers [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].
Never adjust your personal minimums to complete a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

callout.text: A ferry pilot found he would land with only 10 minutes of fuel in marginal weather. He asked: is the schedule more important than an intact airplane? He made a fuel stop [[30:11|RMH Figure 1-2]].

body.p: As an employee you will feel this pressure from a boss or customer. In the RMH example, a pilot with 4 hours of sleep refused a 750-mile trip in marginal weather; the boss was unhappy at first, then agreed [[30:11|RMH Figure 1-2]]. The rule backs you: the PIC is the final authority [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]].

check.q: A charter customer says, "The last pilot flew us in worse weather than this." What does the RMH suggest you rely on?
check.a: Your written personal minimums. Professional pilots live by the numbers, and a written set makes it easier to explain a tough decision to passengers [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Don't change them to complete this flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

chunks.title: Aviation security on the ramp and in the air

body.p: Paying passengers often don't know the ramp. Tell them to move only as directed. If they aren't under your direct supervision, they need an escort for their safety and for ramp security. Supervise baggage loading too [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

bullets: SIDAs are limited-access areas that need an airport-issued badge. Entering without authorization and displayed ID is prohibited [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]].
People entering a SIDA without ID may be reported to the TSA or airport security and face fines. Brief your passengers [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].
Report suspicious activity to the TSA through AOPA's Airport Watch Program, 866-427-3287 [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].
Show your airman and medical certificates to the TSA when asked (49 CFR 1540) [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].
Check NOTAMs for TFRs and National Security Areas while planning. Pilots who don't follow national security rules may be intercepted, detained, and interviewed [[34:12|AIM 5-6-2]].
After the flight: install control locks and anti-theft security locks [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. A postflight inspection and proper securing protect the next pilot's flight [[30:22|RMH 3-4]].

callout.text: Add security to your passenger briefing: where to walk, where not to go, and to stay with you on the ramp [[24:51|AFH 2-14]], [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].

check.q: Two tour passengers wander off toward parked airplanes while you finish the preflight. What does the AFH say?
check.a: Passengers not under your direct supervision should have an escort, for their safety and for ramp security [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

bullets: Checking only the annual on a for-hire flight and forgetting the 100-hour [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].
Treating the 10-hour 100-hour allowance as extra flying time. It is only for getting to the inspection [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].
Deferring an item the kind of operation requires, like the landing light on a night flight for hire [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]], [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]].
Stopping at the strainer sample and skipping the tank sumps [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]].
Trusting the gauges without looking in the tanks [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].
Leaving fuel and oil service to line staff with no oversight [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].
Rushing the long glass-panel checklist [[24:42|AFH 2-5]].
Skewing a risk assessment low because the customer is waiting [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].
Treating the preflight assessment as done once the engine starts. The assessment lasts until the airplane is secured [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

callout.text: Anything out of place on the airframe? Talk it over with a properly rated mechanic before you fly [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].

check.q: Why is "I'll just use the 10-hour grace" the wrong answer when the 100-hour comes due in the middle of a tour day?
check.a: The 10 hours may be used only while en route to reach a place where the inspection can be done, and that time counts toward the next 100 hours [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

f5.caption: Figure 3-6. Example of a numerical FRAT.
f5.alt: Risk assessment form with point values: sleep (did not sleep well 2, slept well 0), how do you feel (cold or ill 4, great 0, a bit off 2), weather at termination (VFR 1, MVFR 3, IMC 4), how is the day going (one thing after another 3, great 0), day 1 or night 3, and planning items (rush 3, no hurry 1, used charts and computer 0, computer program for all planning yes 3, weight and balance not verified 3, performance not evaluated 3, passengers not briefed 2). A colored ramp below shows 0 to 10 not complex flight, 10 to 20 exercise caution, 20 to 30 area of concern, then endangerment.

Occasional row: high, serious, green, white. Remote row: serious, then medium (green) across critical and marginal, low under negligible. Improbable row: green except negligible white.

f7.alt: Sectional excerpt around Elkins-Randolph County airport, a magenta airport symbol inside a dashed magenta circle. Its data line reads 1987 *L 45 123.6 with ASOS 119.275 above. Blue obstacle symbols with MSL elevations and AGL heights in parentheses surround it: 2382 (265) and 2496 (265) to the northwest, 3348 (248) UC near towers to the northeast, 2610 (415) to the south, and a group obstacle symbol marked 3631 UC to the west.

scenario.title: The sunset tour
scenario.setup: You are a new commercial pilot, instrument rated, flying nonstop sightseeing tours for an operator that holds the FAA authorization for them. Tonight's tour carries three paying passengers, leaves 30 minutes before sunset, and lands after dark. It follows a ridge with charted towers. You worked a full day at another job first. The airplane's records show 7.5 hours left until its 100-hour inspection; the tour is 1.2 hours. It rained overnight, and your first left-tank sample has clear beads at the bottom. The manager reminds you that refunds cost the company money. One passenger smells strongly of alcohol and is unsteady on his feet.

questions.q: Pilot: how should a full workday before a night tour affect your plan?
questions.a: Run IMSAFE: fatigue may be subtle and degrade decision-making [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]. For fatigue, the RMH suggests raising your ceiling minimum by at least 500 feet, and making an adjustment for each other factor that applies [[30:17|RMH Figure 2-9]]. If you can't mitigate a high risk, it's a no-go [[30:39|RMH 5-1]].

questions.q: Aircraft: is the airplane legal for this paid tour based on its inspection status?
questions.a: Yes. Carrying people for hire needs an annual or 100-hour within the preceding 100 hours of time in service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. With 7.5 hours left and a 1.2-hour tour, you are inside the limit. Also confirm the annual date, ADs, and that the landing light works, since a night flight for hire needs one [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]].

questions.q: Aircraft: what do you do about the water in the fuel?
questions.a: Keep sampling until no water appears; significant or repeated water means maintenance should investigate [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]. Drain every tank sump, not only the strainer, because water can stay in the tanks after the strainer runs clean [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]]. Never take off until all water is out of the fuel system [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]].

questions.q: Environment: how do you handle the ridge and towers after dark?
questions.a: Night makes terrain and obstacles harder to see, and the same terrain that is low risk by day raises the risk at night [[30:26|RMH 3-8]], [[30:27|RMH 3-9]]. Read obstacle MSL tops from the chart [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]], plan an altitude well above them, and avoid towers horizontally by at least 2,000 feet because of guy wires [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4]].

questions.q: External pressure: the manager mentions refunds. How do you handle it?
questions.a: Recognize it: business pressure can make pilots ignore the other hazards [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. Don't adjust your personal minimums to complete a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Manage passenger expectations and offer another time [[30:40|RMH 5-2]]. You are the final authority [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]].

questions.q: Passengers and security: what about the passenger who appears drunk, and the group on the ramp?
questions.a: Except in an emergency, you may not carry a person who appears intoxicated [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(b)]]. Escort the others on the ramp, supervise their bags [[24:51|AFH 2-14]], and brief them on where they may walk [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].

skills.do: Do the full preflight inspection with the AFM/POH checklist (or one based on it), item by item, and explain to the examiner why each item matters and what a defect looks like. No numeric tolerance applies.
skills.practice: Preflight with the checklist in hand on every flight, touching and naming each item. Have your CFI plant a 'defect' (an open fuel cap, a missing placard) and see if you find it [[24:42|AFH 2-5]], [[24:43|AFH 2-6]].

skills.do: Show from the records that the airplane is airworthy (annual, 100-hour if for hire, transponder, ELT, ADs, required documents), and explain how you would handle an inoperative item, including what changes on a flight for hire.
skills.practice: Pull the real logbooks for your checkride airplane and fill in an airworthiness checklist like AFH Figure 2-4 [[24:40|AFH 2-3]]. Talk through two 91.213(d) cases: one day flight not for hire, one night flight for hire [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]], [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]].

skills.do: Tell the examiner how you assessed yourself: capability (qualification, currency, proficiency), IMSAFE, and your personal minimums, and say you are fit for this flight.
skills.practice: Before each lesson, fill out a numerical FRAT like RMH Figure 3-6 and note your score [[30:28|RMH 3-10]]. Review IMSAFE and the capability questions [[30:22|RMH 3-4]], [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

skills.do: Keep checking weather, terrain, obstructions, airports and airspace before and during the flight, and say what would make you divert, delay, or cancel.
skills.practice: Brief one environmental hazard and its mitigation (go around it, above or below it, change the time, or cancel) before each flight [[30:40|RMH 5-2]]. Recheck your risk assessment if anything changes before takeoff [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].

quiz.q: A Standard Airworthiness Certificate stays in effect as long as:
options: The aircraft keeps a current annual and a 100-hour inspection recorded in the logs
It is renewed by the FAA every 24 calendar months after an inspection
Maintenance follows Parts 21, 43 and 91 and the aircraft stays U.S. registered
The same owner keeps the aircraft and it stays based at its home airport
quiz.why: It is in effect indefinitely if the aircraft is maintained under Parts 21, 43 and 91 and is registered in the U.S. [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. That's why you still check the records before each flight [[24:39|AFH 2-2]].

quiz.q: Which flight requires the airplane to have had an annual or 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours of time in service?
options: A solo cross-country to build commercial time
Flying your own airplane to a meeting
A sightseeing tour with paying passengers
A ferry flight with only crew aboard
quiz.why: The 100-hour rule applies when carrying any person, other than a crewmember, for hire, or giving flight instruction for hire in an airplane you provide [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

quiz.q: Your airplane has no MEL. Before a night VFR flight for hire, the landing light fails. What is true?
options: Deactivate it, placard it inoperative, and go on the night flight
Only a mechanic may placard it, then you may go on the night flight
It is fine if the airport has edge lights on the runway and ramp
It can't be deferred; it is required for this kind of flight
quiz.why: One electric landing light is required for night VFR when operated for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]]. Items required by 91.205 for the kind of flight can't be deferred under 91.213(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

quiz.q: According to the PHAK, the principal fuel contaminant is:
options: Water
Dirt from refueling
Rubber particles from seals
Jet fuel mixed with AVGAS
quiz.why: Water is the principal fuel contaminant [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]]. Dirt and small dark rubber specks can also show up in a sample [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

quiz.q: A fuel sample is clear, smells like kerosene, and feels oily. What is it, and why does it matter?
options: 100LL with the dye faded by sunlight; it is safe to use for the flight
Jet fuel; a piston engine may run long enough to take off, then fail
80/87 avgas; it will only cause mild detonation and roughness
Water with dye in it; keep sampling until the sample turns blue
quiz.why: Jet fuel is clear or straw colored, smells like kerosene, and is oily. A piston engine on jet fuel may start, run, and get airborne, then fail catastrophically [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].

quiz.q: Before a paid tour, a passenger appears intoxicated. There is no emergency. What do the rules say?
options: You may carry him if he sits in the back
You may carry him if another passenger watches him
You may not allow him to be carried
You may carry him if he signs a waiver
quiz.why: Except in an emergency, no pilot may allow a person who appears intoxicated to be carried in the aircraft [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(b)]].

quiz.q: Your risk assessment comes out medium (green). What does the RMH say?
options: Cancel unless you can first lower it to low
Go, but still mitigate the risk if you can
Go with no further thought about the risk
Get a second pilot's approval before you go
quiz.why: Medium risk implies a go decision, but the risk should still be mitigated if possible [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].

quiz.q: On a sectional, an obstacle shows 2610 with (415) below it. What does (415) mean?
options: The ground elevation at the obstacle
The obstacle's height above the ground
The minimum safe altitude near it
The obstacle's distance from the airport
quiz.why: The top of the obstacle is shown in feet MSL; the AGL height is in parentheses below it [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]].

quiz.q: How far horizontally does the AIM say to stay from tall skeletal structures like antenna towers?
options: At least 2,000 feet
At least 1,000 feet
At least 1,500 feet
At least 500 feet
quiz.why: Guy wires can reach about 1,500 feet out from a tower, so avoid skeletal structures horizontally by at least 2,000 feet [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4]].

quiz.q: You fly business clients who must be at a meeting by noon. What does the RMH suggest?
options: Lower your minimums slightly for important clients
Leave without a weather briefing to save time
Promise them an on-time arrival
Manage their expectations and plan other travel options
quiz.why: Pilots who fly business associates feel strong external pressure. Manage passenger expectations and plan alternative travel to reduce risk [[30:40|RMH 5-2]]. Never adjust personal minimums to complete a flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

takeaways: Airworthy = conforms to type design + in condition for safe operation, and you, the PIC, decide [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].
For hire adds: second-class medical, the 100-hour, a landing light at night, and flotation gear far over water.
The 10-hour 100-hour allowance is only for flying to the inspection.
Anything 91.205 requires for the kind of flight can't be deferred under 91.213(d).
Check fuel grade by color and smell, drain the strainer and every tank sump, and watch the fueling.
Use PAVE, a FRAT, and the matrix: serious or high risk means no-go unless you mitigate it.
Expect business pressure; written personal minimums and the PIC's final authority are your answer.
cfi_notes: Handbook conflict on fuel substitution: PHAK 7-27 says to use the next higher grade if the proper grade isn't available, while AFH 2-7 says an 80/87 engine runs on 100LL only if approved as an alternate. Both say never use a lower grade. Teach the AFH line: use only grades the AFM/POH and filler-cap placards approve [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]], [[24:44|AFH 2-7]], since you must comply with the AFM operating limitations, markings and placards [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(a)]]. Don't treat the PHAK line as permission to substitute.
PHAK Figure 7-32 labels green fuel as 100 AVGAS, and AFH 2-7 calls the green grade 100/130. Same grade family; don't let students get stuck on the label.

Examiners like for-hire twists: night landing light, flotation gear over water, the 100-hour, and the intoxicated passenger rule. Give the student a private flight and a for-hire flight with the same squawk and make them compare.
Students often misread the 10-hour 100-hour allowance as a grace period for revenue flying. Drill 91.409(b) with real tach times.
Commercial students know IMSAFE well but often skip the RMH capability questions (qualification, currency, proficiency). Ask about proficiency in the checkride airplane's avionics.
Have the student fill out a numerical FRAT for the checkride flight itself and discuss matrix skewing: wanting the checkride done is an external pressure.
Use the Elkins sectional to practice reading obstacle MSL and AGL numbers, then ask for a safe night altitude along the ridge.
gaps: Airplane-specific items (checklist order, number and location of fuel drains, approved fuel grades, oil limits, equipment list or KOEL) must come from the training airplane's AFM/POH; the lesson uses the AFH's general guidance.
When a flight for hire needs an air carrier or operating certificate (14 CFR Part 119) is not in the resource set. The lesson uses Part 91 for-hire rules and the 91.147 nonstop tour example only.
14 CFR Part 3 (the 3.5(a) definition of airworthy) is not in the resources; it is cited through AFH 2-1.
Aviation security sources are limited to AIM 2-3-15, AIM 5-6, and AFH ramp and securing guidance. TSA general aviation security guidelines and 49 CFR 1540 itself are not included.
The ACS Skills elements for this Task have no numeric tolerances.

activities.title: Name the pilot hazard
activities.intro: Tap a pilot hazard, then tap the self-check question that goes with it.

pairs.r: Do I hold the certificate and ratings this flight needs?
Have I logged the takeoffs, landings and reviews required?
Can I really handle today's conditions, not just legally?
Could that over-the-counter pill have side effects?
Has one good night really fixed a week of short sleep?
Is last night's hangover still with me after 8 hours?

activities.title: Tonight's paid tour: go or fix first?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs. The tour is VFR, for hire, and ends after dark. The airplane has no MEL.

items.t: Left fuel gauge reads empty with fuel in the tank
Annual signed off 13 months ago this week
6 hours left until the 100-hour; the tour is 1.2 hours
Cabin map light dead; not required anywhere; deactivated and placarded

activities.title: True or false: fuel and oil
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: If 100LL isn't available, 80/87 is a fine substitute for an engine that needs 100LL.
cards.why: No. Never substitute a lower grade for a required higher grade; detonation can wreck the engine in a very short time [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].

cards.s: Jet fuel nozzles are flared so they won't fit into an AVGAS filler opening.
cards.why: Yes. AVGAS nozzles are straight; jet fuel nozzles are flared at the end to prevent insertion into AVGAS tanks [[24:45|AFH 2-8]], [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

cards.s: A clean strainer sample proves the tanks have no water.
cards.why: No. Water can stay in the tanks after the strainer shows none. Only the tank sump drains remove it [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]].

cards.s: A new, clean chamois that is already damp will still filter water out of fuel.
cards.why: No. Worn-out chamois don't filter water, and neither will a new, clean chamois that is already water-wet or damp [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]].

cards.s: Filling the tanks after the last flight of the day helps keep water out of the fuel.
cards.why: Yes. The more fuel in the tanks, the less room there is for condensation [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

cards.s: Oil that turns dark quickly in the first few hours after an oil change may point to cylinder problems.
cards.why: Yes. Darkening over time is normal, but rapid darkening right after an oil change may indicate engine cylinder problems [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

activities.title: Read the Elkins sectional
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

activities.title: Run a risk assessment in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: List the hazards in each PAVE category
Rate each hazard's likelihood and severity
Find the composite risk on the matrix
Mitigate each high and serious risk
Assess again until the risk is medium or low
Recheck before takeoff in case hazards changed

activities.title: Work out the numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Use the numerical FRAT (Figure 3-6). You did not sleep well, feel a bit off, and the day has been one thing after another. Destination weather is 4 miles and a 2,500 ft ceiling. The flight is at night and you are rushing. You used charts and a computer to assist (not a program for all planning), checked weight and balance and performance, and will brief passengers. What is the total score?
items.why: Sleep 2 + feel a bit off 2 + one thing after another 3 + MVFR weather 3 + night 3 + rush 3 = 16. Charts and computer 0, program for all planning no 0, weight and balance yes 0, performance yes 0, briefing yes 0. 16 is in the 10 to 20 'exercise caution' range [[30:28|RMH Figure 3-6]].

items.q: A tower on the Elkins sectional is charted 3348 with (248) below it. What is the ground elevation at its base, in feet MSL?
items.why: The top is 3,348 ft MSL and the AGL height in parentheses is 248 ft [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]]. 3,348 - 248 = 3,100 ft MSL.

items.q: In one sectional quadrant the highest feature is a natural peak at 4,862 ft MSL. What MEF, in feet, will the chart show (as a full number)?
items.why: Natural terrain: 4,862 + 100 ft possible error + 200 ft obstacle allowance = 5,162, rounded up to the next 100 = 5,200 ft (charted as 52) [[2:13|Chart Users' Guide p.13]].

items.q: The tour airplane's last 100-hour inspection was at 3,450.0 hours time in service. It now shows 3,538.2. How many hours of paid passenger flying are left before the next 100-hour?
items.why: Next 100-hour due at 3,450.0 + 100 = 3,550.0 [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. 3,550.0 - 3,538.2 = 11.8 hours. The 10-hour allowance is only for flying to the inspection [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

items.q: A night tour lasts 1.4 hours and lands back at the departure airport. The airplane burns 9.5 gallons per hour at normal cruise. What is the minimum fuel, in gallons, needed at takeoff to meet the VFR night reserve? Ignore taxi fuel.
items.why: At night you need enough fuel to reach the first point of intended landing and then fly at least 45 minutes [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(2)]]. 1.4 + 0.75 = 2.15 hours x 9.5 gph = 20.4 gallons.

activities.title: Morning tour, one problem at a time
activities.intro: You are a commercial pilot flying nonstop sightseeing tours for an operator. Your first tour of the day is in N734CA, a Cessna 172 with no MEL. Four paying passengers are due in 45 minutes.

steps.s: The records show the 100-hour comes due in 0.8 hours. The tour is 1.0 hour. The company's other 172 has a current inspection. What do you do?
options: Move the tour to the other 172 after checking its records
Fly N734CA; the annual is current, so that is enough
Fly N734CA; the 10-hour allowance covers the extra 0.2 hours
Fly N734CA and schedule the 100-hour for this afternoon
steps.why: Carrying people for hire requires an annual or 100-hour within the preceding 100 hours. The 10-hour allowance is only for flying to a place where the inspection can be done [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]], [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. Check the other airplane's records before you use it [[24:39|AFH 2-2]].

steps.s: In the other 172, the first sample from the right tank has clear beads at the bottom of the cup. What next?
options: Top off the tank to dilute the water, then fly
Ignore it; a little water is normal after rain
Keep sampling that drain until no water appears
Fly on the left tank only, leaving the right unused
steps.why: Water shows as beads at the bottom of the sample. If you find it in the first sample, continue sampling until no water or contamination appears [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

steps.s: Five more samples from that tank still show water each time. What now?
options: Call it significant water: have maintenance investigate, and delay the tour
Take off; the engine will burn off the small amount of water that may remain in the tank
Run the engine at full power on the ground to clear the water out of the fuel system, then go
Sample the left tank only and go, since the water was found in the right tank
steps.why: Significant or repeated water is grounds for further investigation by qualified maintenance [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]. Never take off until all water and contaminants have been removed from the fuel system [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]].

steps.s: The manager says, "These folks drove two hours. Just go, it's probably fine." What do you do?
options: Go, since the manager accepts the risk and the company is responsible for the flight
Decline, explain the delay, and offer the passengers a later time
Lower your minimums this once, because the passengers have already driven two hours
Go, but fly a shorter route so the passengers are exposed to the weather for less time
steps.why: The manager's push is a business external pressure, and pilots under external pressure sometimes fail to consider the other hazards [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. Manage passenger expectations and offer alternatives [[30:40|RMH 5-2]]. You are the final authority [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]].

steps.s: While maintenance works, the passengers start walking across the ramp to look at a jet. What do you do?
options: Let them; they are paying customers
Call the TSA hotline right away
Tell them to stay clear of propellers and let them go
Escort them back and keep them with you on the ramp
steps.why: Passengers not under your direct supervision should have an escort for their safety and ramp security [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. Brief them on where they may go [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane's annual was done November 3, 2025. Today is November 28, 2026, and the 100-hour has 15 hours left. May you fly a 1-hour paid tour today?
options: No. The annual ran out on November 3, 2026, a year after it was completed.
Yes, but only with no more than two passengers, as the 100-hour is close to due.
No. A for-hire airplane needs an annual every 6 months, so it has already lapsed.
Yes. The annual is good through November 30, 2026, and the 100-hour is current.
final_quiz.why: Twelve calendar months run to the last day of the same month the next year, so November 30, 2026 [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]], [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]]. With 15 hours left, the 100-hour is also current [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

final_quiz.q: A mechanic replaced and rigged an aileron cable, which may have changed how the airplane flies. Before your next paid tour, what must happen?
options: Nothing beyond the mechanic's logbook entry
A pilot with at least a private certificate flies it, checks it, and logs the flight, unless ground tests show conclusively that nothing changed
An FAA inspector must fly it first
You may carry passengers if you tell them about the repair
final_quiz.why: No one but crew may be carried after maintenance that may have appreciably changed flight characteristics until an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private certificate flies it, makes an operational check, and logs it [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]]. The flight isn't needed if ground tests or inspection conclusively show no change [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(c)]].

final_quiz.q: After a cold night you can't get any fuel to flow from one sump drain, and you suspect ice. What does the PHAK suggest?
options: Start the engine to warm the fuel system, then go once fuel flows at any drain
Skip that drain and sample the other sumps, since it is only a local problem
Add extra fuel to push the water out through the drain, then sample the sumps again
Put the airplane in a warm hangar, then drain and check all sumps before flight
final_quiz.why: Free water frozen on the bottom of tanks and filters can make drains useless and later melt into the system. Place the airplane in a warm hangar, then activate and check all sumps and drains before flight [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]].

final_quiz.q: A night tour is planned for 1.2 hours at 11 gallons per hour, returning to the same airport. What is the minimum fuel at takeoff that meets the VFR reserve rule? Ignore taxi fuel.
options: 21.5 gallons
18.7 gallons
13.2 gallons
24.2 gallons
final_quiz.why: At night you need fuel to the first point of intended landing plus at least 45 minutes [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(2)]]. (1.2 + 0.75) x 11 = 21.45, about 21.5 gallons. 18.7 uses the 30-minute day reserve.

final_quiz.q: On the FRAT in the figure: you slept well and feel great, the day is going great, destination weather is better than 5 miles and 3,000 ft, the flight is at night, you are in no hurry, you used charts and a computer to assist (not a program for all planning), you checked weight and balance and performance, and you did not plan to brief passengers. What score and range is that?
options: 7: not complex flight
10: exercise caution
12: exercise caution
4: not complex flight
final_quiz.why: Weather 1 + night 3 + no hurry 1 + no passenger briefing 2 = 7. The other items score 0. 0 to 10 is 'not complex flight' [[30:28|RMH Figure 3-6]]. Briefing your passengers would lower it to 5.

final_quiz.q: Using the matrix in the figure, a hazard is 'remote' but its outcome would be 'catastrophic.' What should you do?
options: Go; remote hazards are always low risk, however severe the outcome
Treat it as serious: no-go unless mitigation brings it to medium or low
Go; it is medium risk and needs no action beyond a normal briefing
Treat it as high: cancel, because mitigation can never lower catastrophic risk
final_quiz.why: Remote likelihood with catastrophic severity is serious (yellow) on the matrix. Serious implies no-go unless you reduce the risk so the next assessment is medium or low [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].

final_quiz.q: The sectional shows a tower charted 2382 with (265) below it. If you fly directly over it at 2,500 ft MSL, about how high are you above the ground at its base?
options: 118 ft
265 ft
383 ft
final_quiz.why: Ground at the base = 2,382 - 265 = 2,117 ft MSL [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]]. 2,500 - 2,117 = 383 ft. You'd clear the top by only 118 ft, and the AIM urges extreme caution below 2,000 ft AGL near towers [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your second-class medical exam isn't due for months, but last week a doctor diagnosed a condition that would keep you from meeting second-class standards. May you fly a paid tour?
options: Yes, until the medical certificate expires
No. You may not act as PIC while you know of a disqualifying condition
Yes, if you feel well today
Yes, if you fly only day VFR
final_quiz.why: You may not act as PIC while you know or have reason to know of a medical condition that would make you unable to meet the medical certificate the flight needs [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]]. Commercial privileges need at least a second-class medical [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]].

final_quiz.q: Before a paid tour you find the stall warning inoperative. It is not deferrable, and no mechanic or parts are available at this airport. What is the legal way to move the airplane to a shop?
options: Placard it INOP and fly the tour on the way
Fly it there yourself with no paperwork
Have a passenger who is a pilot watch the airspeed
Get a special flight permit from the FSDO
final_quiz.why: Items that can't be deferred, such as a stall warning device, must be repaired before departure. If maintenance or parts aren't available, a special flight permit from the FSDO allows a flight to another location for maintenance [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]], [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]].

final_quiz.q: The figure shows a jet fuel nozzle. If jet fuel gets into a piston engine's tanks anyway, what is the main hazard?
options: It won't start at all, so it is only an inconvenience
It runs rough on the ground, so you will always catch it in the run-up
It may run well enough to take off, then fail after takeoff
It only shortens the oil change interval
final_quiz.why: A piston engine on jet fuel may start, run, and power the airplane long enough to get airborne, only to fail catastrophically after takeoff [[24:44|AFH 2-7]]. That is why jet nozzles are flared [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

final_quiz.q: During flight planning for a tour near a large stadium event, what does the AIM say about TFRs?
options: Check NOTAMs in planning; violators of security rules may be intercepted and detained
TFRs apply only to IFR flights, so a VFR tour does not need to check for restrictions near a stadium
ATC will warn you in flight, so you don't need to check NOTAMs during planning for the stadium event
TFRs only affect airplanes over 12,500 pounds, so a light single-engine airplane may fly through them
final_quiz.why: Under 91.103 you must know all available information; pilots are responsible for TFRs and should check NOTAMs during planning [[34:12|AIM 5-6-2]]. Pilots who don't follow national security procedures may be intercepted, detained, and interviewed [[34:12|AIM 5-6-2]].

final_quiz.q: On the walk-around you find the wet compass cloudy with a bubble in the fluid. What is true?
options: It is fine if it still points north, as the cloudy face is cosmetic
You may top it off with fluid yourself and fly
It is only a problem for IFR, as day VFR needs no compass
The compass is unusable, and it is required for day VFR
final_quiz.why: A cloudy face, bubbles, or a partly filled case makes the compass unusable [[24:42|AFH 2-5]]. A magnetic direction indicator is required for day VFR [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: Your tour passengers drove three hours and the weather is just below your written personal minimums. Which statement fits RMH guidance best?
options: Keep your minimums; adjust them only later, with time and objectivity, and with a CFI's input
Fly, but stay closer to the airport
Adjust your minimums today since the passengers came so far
Let the passengers vote on whether to go
final_quiz.why: Don't adjust personal minimums to complete a specific flight. Consider changes only when time and objectivity allow honest self-analysis, and consult a flight instructor before a significant change [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].
